# Independent audit: bounded double-core support triangle and exact compression

Source: `candidate fd39a28eeb41e9c4`.

**Result: full PASS.** The statements are ordinary planar geometry and do not preserve mixed-fiber compatibility.

## 1. Actual support lines and recession geometry

Equality of a sector area to its core triangle forces equality of the compact convex sector sets: proper enlargement of a full-dimensional convex triangle has positive area. A point beyond its bridge line would, by joining it to an interior point of the bridge segment, create points beyond that line inside the same sector. Thus the three bridge lines really support the entire original body.

The halfplane equations and the sector identities q_j+q_l=k-X_i+Y_i check directly. Under the strict half-cap ceiling, every unique sector satisfies X_i>Y_i.

For an unbounded intersection of the three bridge halfplanes, a normalized unbounded sequence produces a nonzero recession direction. No such direction lies in a closed double cone, since its bridge functional is positive on every nonzero vector in that cone. After cyclic relabeling it is (s,-u), s>u>0, and the first and third bridge inequalities give alpha<=u/s<=1-beta. Hence alpha,beta>0 and alpha+beta<=1 exactly.

## 2. Neighboring envelope calculations and contradiction

For unique sector 2, the proposed coordinates have determinant Bt. The two inequalities become u+mv<=1 and v-nu<=1 with m>0, m<=1, n>=-1 and determinant D_2/ell>0. Their four stated vertices, including the coincident-vertex boundary cases, are correct and yield formula (5). For sector 3 the determinant is ab, the second coefficient w is positive, s,w<=1, and 1-sw=D_3>0. The same quadrant calculation yields formula (6), even when s is negative. The unused third halfplane only decreases the actual sector, so the upper envelopes are valid.

Multiplying the two strict lower area requirements and adding eliminates the mixed coefficients exactly as stated. After division by a, the right-minus-left expression is

    (B-beta t)^2/t+(b-alpha a)^2/a
       +(1-alpha-beta)(beta t+alpha a).

All terms are nonnegative in the recession regime, contradicting the strict requirement. Thus the support intersection is bounded. A bounded full-dimensional intersection of three halfplanes is a triangle, and each cutting ray is stopped at its actual endpoint by one of these bridge inequalities. This verifies the same-six-endpoints conclusion.

## 3. Finite corner replacement

For a triangle with three strict distinct-vertex cuts, its six-ray hull removes precisely three disjoint unique corner triangles, up to null boundaries. If an intermediate convex body contains that hull and the other two triangle vertices, it contains the whole triangle except possibly the remaining unique corner: take the convex hull of the six-ray hull with those two vertices.

Removing a homothetic corner of scale sqrt(E/L) produces exactly the original missing area in that same unique sector. It keeps the six-ray hull and changes no other sector. Hence all six endpoint locations and sector areas, every full central chord, the three cap areas, and the row values agree exactly. The full-scale cut retains P and Q; zero loss is handled by the triangle itself. No smallness, smoothness, or continuity argument is needed.

## 4. Application to the alternating three-positive-edge pentagon

In the (2S,2S,2D) pattern, the positive edges alternate. If they were the double sectors, the three unique sectors would be their cores. Their core product equals the product of the three double core areas, contradicting X_i>Y_i>=the respective double core areas. Thus the positive edges are the unique sectors and all three double bridges are cores.

The support triangle exists by the preceding theorem. Positive unique excess ensures that its three vertices are strictly in their distinct unique sectors. At either singular two-node block, zero node slacks force the inserted vertex onto both adjacent bridge lines, hence onto the corresponding support-triangle vertex. The exact sector area equals the full triangle sector area. Since the original actual sector is a compact convex subset with equal area, it is the whole sector and contains that vertex. This avoids the false inference that an arbitrary replacement vertex must belong to the original body.

The original body therefore differs from the support triangle in at most one unique corner, and the exact compression gives a quadrilateral with identical data. This validly removes the need for a separate row argument in that pentagon branch. It proves neither a row inequality on all remaining quadrilaterals nor a general triangle reduction.
